item.title: Environmental dynamics and timing of the late Eemian interglacial to the Weichselian pleniglacial at Lichtenberg, Germany: implications for the Oerel and Glinde interstadials
item.dc:creator: Alexis Badai Samudra, Michael Hein, Martin Theuerkauf, Neda Rahimzadeh, Marcel Weiss, David Colin Tanner, … (+1)
item.description:
Boreas — matched: Greenland, interglacial, Eemian, MIS stage, proxy, sediment core, radiocarbon
The terrestrial sediment archives of northern Germany provide important insights into Late Pleistocene climate variability, but continuous and well‐dated records remain rare. In particular, the age and stratigraphic position of the Oerel and Glinde interstadials within the Early Weichselian to pleniglacial transition remain poorly constrained. These interstadials are commonly attributed to MIS 3, but this assignment is uncertain due to limited numerical dating, reliance on biostratigraphic correlation and the limitations of radiocarbon dating near its upper range. This study presents a new, high‐resolution multi‐proxy record (sedimentology, geochemistry, palynology) from two sediment cores at Lichtenberg, Lower Saxony, positioned directly next to a multi‐phased Middle Palaeolithic archaeological site and supported by a robust chronology based on new optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) ages. The record documents the vegetation and landscape dynamics from the late Eemian interglacial into the Weichselian pleniglacial, capturing major climatic transitions and the onset of cold, periglacial conditions. Within this sequence, we identify two previously unresolved climatic oscillations (Dangenstorf I and II), characterised by expansions of Betula nana ‐shrub tundra and increased organic accumulation. Based on pollen assemblages and OSL dating, these oscillations are correlated with the Oerel and Glinde interstadials, which are themselves stratigraphically positioned between the Odderade interstadial and the onset of the Weichselian pleniglacial. Furthermore, our OSL chronology places them firmly within the MIS 5a/4 transition. We assign them to the Greenland interstadials (GI) 20 and 19.2, respectively, rather than to MIS 3 as previously assumed. The Lichtenberg record thus provides a continuous, well‐dated archive that redefines the chronostratigraphy of the Early Weichselian to pleniglacial transition in northern Germany and strengthens its correlation with North Atlantic climate variability.

item.title: Resolving short-term meteorological variability amplifies projected glacier loss and sea-level rise
item.dc:creator: Lander Van Tricht, Matthias Huss, Harry Zekollari, Rodrigo Aguayo, Janosch Beer, Marit van Tiel, … (+2)
item.description:
Nature Communications — matched: glacier, mass loss, sea level, sea-level rise, parameterization, ensemble
Abstract Global glacier models typically rely on temperature-index mass balance calculations forced with aggregated meteorological data, limiting their ability to resolve short-term variability. Here, we develop a daily-resolution version of the Global Glacier Evolution Model (GloGEM), which we apply globally and compare against the monthly configuration. Our results show that the daily model more closely reproduces mass balance observations and provides a more detailed representation of glacier runoff. Accounting for short-term meteorological variability leads to systematically greater projected mass loss, with up to 25% greater loss in Svalbard. These differences arise from extreme melt days, precipitation-phase transitions, and surface-type feedbacks not fully represented at monthly resolution. Globally, the daily model yields ice volume losses of 26 ± 10% under low-emission and 47 ± 17% under high-emission scenarios over 2025-2100 (ensemble mean ± 1 StD), resulting in an additional 5-10% mass loss (20-33 mm of global mean sea-level rise) relative to the monthly implementation. Resolving high-frequency forcing, or accounting for its effects through parameterisations, is therefore essential for robust glacier projections, while its omission may systematically underestimate future glacier loss.

item.title: ACE2-NEMO: Coupling an ML atmospheric emulator to a full-depth dynamical ocean model
item.dc:creator: Bobby Antonio, Kristian Strommen, Pablo Ortega, Hannah M. Christensen
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: Earth system model, Earth system, coupled climate model, greenhouse gas, CO2, emulator
arXiv:2603.28704v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding how fast atmospheric variability shapes slow climate variability and sensitivity remains a central challenge in Earth-system science. Recent advances in machine-learned (ML) atmospheric models have demonstrated remarkable skill on weather timescales, but their emergent behaviour in a fully coupled climate system remains largely unexplored. We present early results from a new hybrid modelling framework, in which the ACE2 ML atmospheric emulator is interactively coupled to the NEMO ocean model. We report on a set of 70-year coupled simulations (1950-2020 historical forcing and fixed-1950s control). These experiments represent, to our knowledge, one of the first multi-decadal integrations of a machine-learned atmosphere interacting with a full-depth dynamical ocean. Several historical and fixed-1950s control simulations from the fully dynamic global coupled climate model EC-Earth, which has the same ocean component used in ACE2-NEMO, are also considered for comparison. We assess the behaviour of the coupled system, with particular focus on low-frequency tropical variability and the climate response to greenhouse-gas forcing. Analysis of potentially emergent El Nino-like variability reveals realistic fast timescale air-sea coupling in the tropical Pacific, but the temporal variability is unrealistic, with very low amplitude oscillations; this appears to be due to weak atmospheric feedback in the tropical Pacific. The response to CO2 forcing shows initial agreement with EC-Earth3P but deviates due to reduced downward short-wave radiation in ACE2. These results provide a unique test of physical realism and generalisability for atmospheric emulators and evaluate the possible role of entirely machine-learned components in next-generation Earth system models.

item.title: Progressive changes in geometry and dynamics of the Northern Pine Island Ice Shelf, West Antarctica
item.dc:creator: Yite Chien, Chunxia Zhou, Baojun Zhang
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: ice shelf, Antarctic, Antarctica
The Northern Pine Island Ice Shelf plays an important role in slowing the flow of Antarctic ice into the ocean, but its changes have been poorly understood. Using satellite observations and environmental data collected over several decades, we found that this ice shelf has thinned, retreated, and lost contact with the seabed. These changes suggest the ice shelf is becoming less stable and highlights the importance of continued monitoring to anticipate potential disintegration.

item.title: TerraNostra-Bench: Benchmarking Spatial Downscaling and Temporal Rollout for Global 1-km Land-Use Reconstruction
item.dc:creator: Amirpasha Mozaffari, Marina Casta\~no, Stefano Materia, Joan Vedr\'i, Jordi Varela-Agrelo, Dario Garcia-Gasulla, … (+3)
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: carbon cycle, Earth system model, Earth system, downscaling
arXiv:2610.27793v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Uncertainty in the terrestrial carbon cycle remains a major constraint in climate projections, partly due to imperfect land surface representations in Earth system models. We propose a data-driven framework for high-resolution land-use reconstruction, treated as a semantic-segmentation task, that combines coarse-resolution scenario data and climate classification with static geophysical features to produce annual land-use maps at 1 km resolution. We introduce TerraNostra-Bench, a change-aware evaluation protocol that separates spatial downscaling from autoregressive temporal rollout and scores models on the rare land-use-change pixels rather than the dominant static background. Using it, we compare convolutional (U-Net) and transformer (Swin) backbones in autoregressive and non-autoregressive schemes against persistence, linear, and shallow convolutional baselines. The autoregressive prior is the most informative input yet accumulates error over long rollouts: autoregressive models lose 5.7-7.2 accuracy points over 13 years, against 2.2-2.8 for non-autoregressive models. This trade-off is governed by the autoregressive choice rather than the backbone. It can be tuned by an inference-time prior-trust threshold that requires no retraining and by the training-time weighting of reconstruction and change objectives; the two levers trace complementary frontiers, with calibration recovering up to 10 accuracy points while keeping change sensitivity above the persistence floor. Extrapolating beyond the training window, backward to 1955-1959 and forward to 2015-2019 under scenario forcing, the models retain most of their in-window skill and show the same trade-off, indicating it is intrinsic to the design. This work provides the methodological foundation and evaluation surface for a forthcoming temporally continuous land-use product.

item.title: GlaUnTI: a hybrid physics–machine learning model enables transferable glacier surface mass balance estimation
item.dc:creator: Konstantin A. Maslov, Thomas Schellenberger, Claudio Persello, Alfred Stein
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: glacier, surface mass balance, machine learning
Glaciers are melting worldwide, but direct measurements are spatially sparse. We developed a new model that combines mechanistic physical rules with machine learning to better estimate yearly gains and losses of ice mass across Europe. By learning local corrections to a physical melt model, the machine learning component improves accuracy and works well on glaciers not used for training. This will help produce more reliable glacier assessments and support future climate studies.

item.title: Decadal changes in the monthly variance and persistence of simulated Antarctic sea ice anomalies
item.dc:creator: Marika M. Holland, Alice K. DuVivier, Will R. Hobbs, Laura Landrum, Marilyn Raphael, Sharon E. Stammerjohn
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: Antarctic, sea ice, Earth system model, Earth system
Abstract During the last decade, Antarctic sea ice area has undergone dramatic change, and anomalies have become much larger and longer-lived relative to earlier in the satellite record. These changes in sea ice variance and persistence have led to the suggestion that a regime change may have occurred in the Antarctic system. Using simulations from a coupled Earth system model, we diagnose the factors that give rise to decadal-scale changes in the variance and persistence of Antarctic sea ice anomalies that arise from internal climate variability. The model simulates changes in these properties that are comparable to observed variations. In decades with highly variable and longer-lived (persistent) sea ice anomalies, larger anomalies in total Southern Hemisphere ice area result from a reduced regional compensation of sea ice variations. This is associated with differences in the Southern Annular Mode (SAM) spatial structure and consequent differences in wind-driven ice area anomalies. The higher persistence of sea ice anomalies in these decades results in part from changes in the Weddell Sea where ice variations are more strongly driven by subsurface ocean temperature anomalies. These simulated decadal-scale differences arise from internal variability, suggesting that anthropogenic forcing is not a necessary condition for the increased variance and persistence of Antarctic sea ice anomalies observed in recent decades.

item.title: Chronology of the short-term climate changes during the Holocene in northwestern Russia and its correlation with the solar activity variations
item.dc:creator: Khikmat A. Arslanov, Valentin A. Dergachev, Ф. Е. Максимов, I. V. Kudryavtsev, Yaroslav V. Kuzmin
item.description:
Radiocarbon — matched: glacier, polar, Holocene, cosmogenic, radiocarbon
Abstract A more accurate radiocarbon dating of short-period climate changes in the Holocene requires to take into account short-term changes in variation of the 14 C concentration in the atmosphere, which could lead to a dating error of up to 300 years. To eliminate this potential problem, Bronk Ramsey’s model was used, based on a comparison of the radiocarbon dates with the calibration curve. Using this model, a corrected (i.e., modeled) age was established for the entire series of previously determined radiocarbon dates obtained from the Nikolsko-Lyutinskoye, Shirinsky Mokh, and Sambalskoye raised bog sections in northwestern European Russia. The deviations of the average annual temperature from its modern value (∆T), presented in previous publications as graphs, were converted into digital form. Using this model, a refined calendar chronology was established. The chronology of short-period climate changes in the Holocene demonstrates the synchronicity of short-term climate fluctuations. In most cases, it agrees well with the chronology obtained in the study of natural objects (lakes, bogs, marine sediments, and polar glaciers), as well as with the advances of mountain glaciers. The chronology of short-period climate changes is compared to the changes in solar activity, established by using concentrations of cosmogenic isotopes: 14 C in tree rings, and 10 Be in polar glaciers. The synchronicity of short-term climate fluctuations and variations of solar activity in the Holocene has been established, and it suggests that changes of solar activity are one of the main causes of short-period climate fluctuations in the Holocene.

item.title: Exploring Recent Changes in Tornado Activity via an Environment-based Tornado Count Model for CMIP6 Applications
item.dc:creator: Kelsey Malloy, Tyler Fricker, Zoe Schroder, Daniel Burow
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: model intercomparison, CMIP, reanalysis, climate change
Abstract Tornadoes cause extreme, localized loss of life and property. Therefore, it is of societal importance to understand how tornado activity may be influenced by climate and climate change. Because climate models do not explicitly resolve tornadoes, tornado-relevant environments are often used to detect tornado trends and project future changes in tornado activity with climate model output. However, when making long-term tornado projections, it is essential to assess how biases in these tornado-relevant environments within climate models affect tornado count estimates. In this study, we developed a tornado count model that uses large-scale monthly environments to predict monthly tornado counts, which is trained with observational environments and reports but is calibrated for use with Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP) version 6 environments. We found that convective precipitation for most CMIP6 models is too low, and the environment-based tornado count model has seasonal cycle errors, e.g., too high tornado activity in summer. After correcting for these issues, the CMIP6 tornado count model well represents the historical seasonal cycle and spatial distribution of U.S. tornado activity in terms of average and extreme (90th percentile) annual tornado counts. In addition, we estimated recent increases in tornado activity, particularly over the lower Mississippi River Valley, consistent with observational reports. While the spatial pattern of changes in tornado activity from CMIP6 aligns broadly with reports and reanalysis environments, the model with CMIP6 environments estimates a smaller magnitude in recent trends, suggesting most of recent upward trends reflect internal variability. A modest portion of recent upward tornado trends may be driven by external forcing of convective environments.

item.title: A Review of Chinese Attempts in Ice Drilling Technology
item.dc:creator: Xinlong Che, Yazhou Li, Xiaopeng Fan, Da Gong, Bing Li, Pavel G. Тalalay, … (+5)
item.category: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
item.description:
Journal of Marine Science and Engineering — matched: subglacial, Antarctica, polar
China has made considerable efforts in its ice-drilling technology since the 1970s; however, a comprehensive overview of its achievements is still lacking. This paper reviews China’s progress in ice-drilling technology over the past five decades. First, drilling projects in the Third Pole and polar regions are summarized. In the Third Pole region, more than 120 boreholes have been drilled, with the deepest reaching 324 m and the highest on the summit of Mount Everest. In Antarctica, Chinese drilling activities have mainly been concentrated in the area near Great Wall Station and along the traverse from Zhongshan Station to Dome A. Key achievements include a >800 m deep ice-core borehole at Dome A, a 3413 m hot-water borehole at Qilin Subglacial Lake (QSL), and the recovery of two subglacial bedrock cores. Second, the mechanical and thermal ice drills developed in China are reviewed. Before the 2010s, China had only shallow-drilling systems. Since then, a series of ice drills with deep-drilling capabilities have been developed. Future drilling priorities include resuming deep coring at Dome A, exploring QSL, sampling the subglacial bedrock of the Gamburtsev Subglacial Mountains (GSMs), and expanding activities to West Antarctica. Simultaneously, existing drills that are still at the laboratory or early field-testing phase require further refinement and validation, and the development of new drills, such as a deep ice-core drill, a thermal ice coring drill, and a flexible-tube air reverse-circulation drill, should be actively pursued.

item.title: Northern Hemisphere Snow Cover Dynamics over the Past Half-Century: A Bibliometric Synthesis (1977–2025)
item.dc:creator: Xiaona Chen, Xuebin Meng, Yang Xu
item.description:
Remote Sensing — matched: cryosphere, radiative forcing, remote sensing, global warming
As a fundamental component of the Earth’s climate system, snow cover critically mediates surface radiative forcing, terrestrial water storage, and large-scale atmospheric momentum exchange. Its long-term trends are a direct fingerprint of global warming, yet the scientific literature on snow cover dynamics has grown exponentially, posing substantial challenges for systematic knowledge synthesis. To map the intellectual landscape of Northern Hemisphere (NH) snow cover dynamics, we conducted a comprehensive bibliometric review of this corpus based on 10,350 peer-reviewed articles retrieved from the Web of Science. The bibliometric analysis reveals a sustained upward trajectory in publication output, with core journals concentrated in Remote Sensing, Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres, and The Cryosphere, and leading research institutions represented by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, the French National Centre for Scientific Research, and the University of Colorado Boulder. Methodologically, this field is shifting toward the integration of high-resolution remote sensing with intelligent algorithms. Geographically, research hotspots are predominantly located in high-mountain areas, with additional focus on typical snow zones across North America, Europe, Russia, Central Asia, and the Tibetan Plateau. Despite ongoing advances in remote sensing and algorithmic techniques, the synergistic integration of multi-source snow data and the operational production of long-term, high-resolution hemispheric snow cover products remain critical bottlenecks that urgently need to be addressed. These findings provide valuable references for optimizing future snow monitoring systems and advancing model development.

item.title: BridgeCast: Bridging Ocean Wave Forecasts to Reanalysis via Flow Matching with Exogenous Variables
item.dc:creator: Siyu Gan, Dongsheng Luo, Kunxiaojia Yuan, Dongjin Song, Jingchao Ni
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: reanalysis, parameterization
arXiv:2610.03759v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ocean wave forecasting is essential for maritime safety, offshore operations, and coastal resilience, yet remains challenging due to systematic biases in physics-based models. Physical models, while widely used, rely on approximations and parameterizations that limit their accuracy under complex ocean-atmosphere conditions. To enhance ocean wave forecasting, we propose BridgeCast, within a physics-AI hybrid framework for bias correction. BridgeCast is a probabilistic model based on conditional flow matching (CFM) that learns to transform physical model forecasts into reanalysis-like fields. It treats physical forecasts as corrupted observations and employs a continuous-time generative process to bridge their distribution toward that of reanalysis data. BridgeCast is parameterized by a Transformer-based architecture that enables spatiotemporal modeling, incorporation of exogenous atmospheric variables, and flexible inference via both ordinary and stochastic differential equation formulations. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that BridgeCast consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across regions and forecast lead times.

item.title: Clarifying tipping terminology
item.dc:creator: Niklas Boers, Robert E. Kopp, Peter Ashwin, Sebastian Bathiany, Maya Ben-Yami, Reyk B\"orner, … (+19)
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: tipping point, Earth system
arXiv:2610.14930v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The notion of tipping points and related terminology have so far had inconsistent and sometimes confusing definitions in both scientific and popular literature. While it is difficult for the scientific community to align popular usage of the term tipping point with a precise definition, technical usage of related terms would benefit from greater consistency and rigor. Toward this end, we offer a systematic set of terms to clarify formal communication around potential tipping dynamics, with focus on examples from Earth system dynamics.

item.title: Disentangling forced and internal components in observed climate evolution using spatiotemporal deep learning
item.dc:creator: Parvathi Kooloth, Wenyu Zhou, L. Ruby Leung, Shang-Ping Xie, Hailong Wang, Qiang Fu
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: Arctic, ensemble, machine learning, climate change
arXiv:2610.28219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attribution of observed historical climate evolution to externally forced change and internal variability is fundamental to understanding climate change and evaluating climate models. Yet such attribution remains challenging because the forced response is intertwined with internal variability in observations. Here, we develop a convolutional long short-term memory network (ConvLSTM) to disentangle these two components. Trained and evaluated using large-ensemble simulations from multiple climate models, ConvLSTM consistently outperforms existing model-based, statistical, and machine-learning approaches. Applying ConvLSTM to observations reveals an evolving spatial pattern of the forced response and substantial contributions from internal variability to recent multidecadal climate trends. For several key climate features whose attribution remains debated, ConvLSTM indicates that internal variability amplified the forced reversal of Atlantic interhemispheric temperature asymmetry, dominated the observed La Ni\~na-like warming pattern over the equatorial Pacific and the associated precipitation decline over southwestern North America since 1980, and modulated Arctic amplification around its nearly constant threefold forced value. Comparison between the ConvLSTM-estimated and model-simulated forced responses reveals broadly consistent patterns but also important discrepancies, with climate models simulating stronger Northern Hemisphere warming, weaker subtropical high intensification, and smaller land precipitation declines. Overall, ConvLSTM provides a robust framework for attributing historical climate evolution and evaluating the fidelity of climate models

item.title: Nonlinear Amplification of Summer Extreme Heat Events in Northeast China and Mongolia by the Preceding Winter Northeast Pacific Cold Blob and Spring Indo-Pacific Warm Pool SST
item.dc:creator: Hao Wang, Jianping Li, Fei Zheng, Matthew David Collins, Yinan Yang, Fei Li, … (+2)
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: sea surface temperature, heat extreme
Abstract Summer extreme heat events pose severe risks to society and ecosystems. This study reveals a significant synergistic effect between the preceding winter negative Northeast Pacific sea surface temperature anomalies (nNEP SSTA), known as the “cold blob”, and spring negative Indo-Pacific Warm Pool SST anomalies (nIPWP SSTA), that intensifies summer heat extremes in Northeast China and Mongolia. When co-occurring, these factors nonlinearly amplify heat events far beyond their individual linear effects. The mechanism for this synergistic effect involves a series of coupled oceanic and atmospheric bridges. The two factors jointly generate spring anomalous westerlies that sustain the nNEP SSTA into summer via the Wind-Evaporation-SST feedback. This persistent summer anomaly triggers eastward propagating Rossby waves energy, establishing a strong local anticyclone and increased atmospheric thickness over Northeast China and Mongolia, which directly increases the temperature of the atmospheric layer and favors extreme heat events. Furthermore, this circulation induces soil moisture deficits, further intensifying the heat through soil moisture feedback. These nonlinear processes are confirmed by General circulation model experiments. These findings highlight the importance of the synergistic influence of these remote SST anomalies for the prediction of summer heat extremes over Northeast China and Mongolia.

item.title: Indian Ocean Dipole Impacts on Autumn Heat and Early-Winter Precipitation over the Arabian Peninsula
item.dc:creator: Yiling Zheng, Hari Prasad Dasari, Dingrui Cao, Raju Attada, Ibrahim Hoteit
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: heat wave
Abstract The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) exerts a season-spanning influence on Arabian Peninsula (AP) climate, modulating both autumn (September–November, SON) heat and early-winter (October–December, OND) precipitation. During positive IOD, the southern AP warms in SON via a radiative pathway: anomalous low-level moisture transport enhances the greenhouse effect, strengthening downward longwave radiation and diabatic heating. As conditions cool into OND, the IOD’s influence pivots to precipitation. Positive IOD amplifies OND precipitation through two mechanisms: a low-level moisture conveyor leads to convergence-dominated precipitation along the southwestern coast, while a strengthened subtropical jet interacts with this moistening environment in the northeast. In contrast, negative IOD features weaker, spatially distinct SON cooling centered over the northern AP, primarily from cold-air advection, and broadly suppressed OND precipitation. These seasonal mean shifts would alter the probability of high-impact weather. On synoptic timescales, the enhanced moisture during positive IOD can first radiatively amplify heatwaves and then fuel extreme precipitation within days. This dual fingerprint clarifies the IOD’s role in AP climate variability and provides a physical basis for assessing compound heat-rainfall hazards in a warming world.

item.title: HTAP3-OPNS: ozone, PM, nitrogen and sulphur deposition – multi-model experiments to support the revision of the CLRTAP Gothenburg Protocol
item.dc:creator: Tim Butler, Tabish Ansari, Claudio A. Belis, Elisa Bergas-Masso, Willem van Caspel, Hilde Fagerli, … (+20)
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
Air pollution travels across continents, meaning emissions in one region can affect air quality far away. To better understand this, scientists from many groups are planning to run coordinated computer simulations of the atmosphere. By comparing results across models and emission scenarios, the planned study will show how pollution moves between regions and which sources matter most, helping governments design more effective air quality policies.
